name: Ba'athism
info: Ba'athism is an Arab nationalist ideology of a unified Arab state ruled by a vanguard party under revolutionary socialism; it arose in Syria in the 1940s and shaped the one-party regimes of Syria and Iraq.

facts.thinkers: Michel Aflaq, generally counted its founder or chief contributor; Salah al-Din al-Bitar, who worked directly with Aflaq; Zaki al-Arsuzi, who influenced Aflaq and founded the Arab Ba'ath; Hafez al-Assad, whose policies gave rise to Assadism; Saddam Hussein, whose politics gave rise to Saddamism
facts.texts: Aflaq's essay compilation Fi Sabil al-Ba'ath (The Road to Renaissance, 1940), the party's main ideological book for more than two decades; the Ba'ath Party Charter of 1947, whose Articles 26–37 set out its socialism
facts.ideas: Arab nationalism and the unity of the Arab nation; baʽth, the renaissance of Arab culture, values and society; a vanguard party ruling for an unspecified time; Arab socialism with state ownership of natural resources and the principal means of production; revolution against the reactionary classes; a secular state with Islam kept spiritual; the slogan "Unity, Freedom, Socialism"
facts.today: Both Ba'athist regimes fell: Iraq's in 2003 and Syria's on 8 December 2024; the Ba'ath party in Syria was dissolved in 2025, few Ba'athist groups remain elsewhere with limited influence, and organisations linked to the party in Lebanon face forced dissolution by the government

t: Ba'athism joined Arab nationalism to a socialism that rejected Marxist class struggle, and held that a vanguard Ba'ath party should rule for an unspecified time to build an "enlightened" Arab society.
The founders' party split in 1966 into a Syrian-dominated and an Iraqi-dominated movement, and the Assad family and Saddam Hussein built personalist dictatorships in the two countries.
Both Ba'athist regimes built police states with mass surveillance and ideological indoctrination, and both fell: Iraq's in the invasion of 2003, Syria's on 8 December 2024.
dyk: Michel Aflaq, a Christian, called the rise of Islam in the seventh century the first Arab renaissance; when he died in 1989 the Iraqi Regional Command announced that he had converted to Islam, but his family was said not to know of any conversion.
ev: Zaki al-Arsuzi founds the Arab Ba'ath on 29 November, and Michel Aflaq and Salah al-Din al-Bitar found the Arab Ihya Movement, later the Arab Ba'ath Movement
The first party congress meets, the two Ba'ath movements merge, and the party adopts its charter
The Military Committee of the Syrian Ba'ath party launches a coup that sets up a one-party state in Syria
A second Syrian coup overthrows the old guard led by Aflaq and Bitar and splits the movement into a Syrian and an Iraqi wing
The Iraqi Ba'ath seizes power in a coup and later gives asylum to Aflaq
The Corrective Revolution puts Hafez al-Assad in power in Syria
The invasion of Iraq topples Saddam Hussein, and the Iraqi Ba'ath party is banned
The Assad regime falls on 8 December, ending Ba'athist rule in Syria

sections.origins:
Ba'athism originated in the political thought of the Syrian philosophers Michel Aflaq, Salah al-Din al-Bitar and Zaki Arsuzi, who are counted as its founders although they formed different organisations. In 1939 they and three others briefly tried to establish a party, which likely failed through personal animosity between Arsuzi and Aflaq. Arsuzi, an Arab from Alexandretta, was inspired by the French Revolution, the German and Italian unification movements and the Japanese economic "miracle", and was influenced by Hegel, Marx, Nietzsche and Oswald Spengler. He founded the Arab National Party in 1939, which dissolved that year, and on 29 November 1940 the Arab Ba'ath.

Aflaq and the more junior Bitar founded the Arab Ihya Movement in 1940, renamed the Arab Ba'ath Movement in 1943. Arsuzi suspected it of being an imperialist plot to undercut his influence by creating a movement of the same name. The two movements sparred over the 1941 coup of Rashid Ali Al-Gaylani in Iraq: Aflaq's backed the government and sent volunteers against the British, while Arsuzi opposed the coup. His party lost members to Aflaq's, and Vichy French authorities expelled him from Syria in 1941. Aflaq's movement held its first party congress in 1947 and merged with Arsuzi's Arab Ba'ath; socialist values, present from the start, were stressed after the merger with Akram Al-Hawrani's Arab Socialist Movement in 1953.
sections.ideas:
Ba'athism advocates a unified Arab state under a Ba'athist vanguard party and a revolutionary socialist framework, in the slogan "Unity, Freedom, Socialism". Aflaq, following Sati' al-Husri, held that language was the principal unifying factor of the Arab nation, and history another. At the centre of his thought was baʽth, "renaissance": the first Arab renaissance had been the emergence of Islam in the seventh century, and a new one would come by uniting the Arab nation. He blamed Arab states' decline on "feudalism, sectarianism, regionalism, intellectual reactionism", and held that only revolutionaries pure and devoted could cure them. Because reactionary classes ruled most Arab states, he later proposed that revolution spread from one country to the next, the transformed countries then uniting.

Aflaq supported a Leninist vanguard party built on democratic centralism, which could initiate policy even against a majority, since the population was still shaped by the old moral system. His liberty was authoritarian: a party that was not elected would ensure it, since the party had the common good at heart. The 1947 Charter placed natural resources, the principal means of production and transport in the hands of the state and abolished foreign concessions. Aflaq admired Marxist tenets but rejected dialectical materialism as the only truth, and held that in the Arab world all classes struggled against foreign capitalist domination. A Christian, he wished Islam to be "not imposed" on state and society, opposed atheism and fundamentalism, and supported secular government.
sections.spread:
Ba'athism took the form of two rival parties, one Syrian-led and one Iraqi-led. After the 1963 coup in Syria, the party that took power was dominated by radical military officers known as the "Neo-Ba'ath", who put the establishment of a socialist state before pan-Arab unity. The coup of 1966 led by Salah Jadid and Hafez al-Assad overthrew the old guard of Aflaq and Bitar, and many Syrian Ba'athist leaders defected to Iraq. Scholar Ofra Bengio claims that the pro-Syrian movement then took Arsuzi as the father of Ba'athist thought, while the pro-Iraqi movement kept Aflaq. Bitar left the movement in 1968, and Aflaq, who remained, became the ideologue of the Iraqi movement but was sidelined politically.

The Syrian government under Jadid stopped working for unity, took up terms such as "class struggle" and "people's war", and drew close to the Syrian Communist Party and the Soviet Union. Hafez al-Assad took power in 1970, and Assadism took shape in Syria; in Iraq Saddamism took shape around Saddam Hussein. Hostilities between the two movements lasted until Hafez al-Assad's death in 2000, after which Bashar al-Assad pursued reconciliation with Iraq. The Syrian party also held influence in Lebanon during Syria's occupation of that country. The National Vanguard Party, tied to the Iraqi Ba'ath party, operated in Mauritania.
sections.power:
Ba'athism ruled in Syria from 1963 and in Iraq after the 1968 coup. The Assad family and Saddam Hussein came to dominate the two parties and built personalist dictatorships. The two regimes built police states that enforced mass surveillance and ideological indoctrination, subordinated student organisations, trade unions and other civil society to the party and the state, pursued Arabisation of ethnic minorities, and legitimised their rule with conspiratorial anti-Zionist and anti-Western sentiment. The 1966 coup in Syria cost approximately 400 lives; the Jadid regime banned religious preaching and persecuted the clergy, whom neo-Ba'athists saw as class enemies.

Hafez al-Assad, after 1970, purged the armed forces, secret police, security forces and bureaucracy and installed loyalists, building a "coup-proof" system on nepotism and ethnic favouritism, with an Alawitisation of the party and the military. Bashar al-Assad's crackdown on the 2011 Syrian revolution was brutal and led to a deadly civil war. The Simon Wiesenthal Center reported that the Nazi war criminal Alois Brunner died in Syria in 2010 under Bashar al-Assad's asylum, having advised both Assads on torture and on purging Syria's Jewish community; the regime rejected such accusations.

In Iraq party documents ordered branches to check the Arabic origin of prospective wives and their families. During the war with Iran the party moved against members of non-Arab, especially Iranian, origin, and Saddam Hussein agreed with a Secretariat recommendation that people of Iranian origin not be admitted.
sections.critiques:
Historian Paul Salem called Aflaq's authoritarian view of liberty, with an unelected party as its guarantor, weak in an "obvious" way, and some, Salem among them, saw his Arab nationalism as romantic and poetic. Aflaq's own followers judged the regimes harshly. Munif al-Razzaz, a former secretary general of the National Command, held that from 1961 there were two parties, a military one that was Ba'athist only in name, and Bitar said the 1966 coup "marked the end of Ba'athist politics in Syria". Aflaq said, "I no longer recognise my party!" Jamal al-Atassi, a co-founder of Arsuzi's party and later a dissident, called Assadism a false nationalism, the domination of a minority, and said its state was run by a class that had made a fortune without contributing.

The historian of fascism Cyprian Blamires holds that Ba'athism may have been a Middle Eastern variant of fascism, pointing to its mix of illiberal nationalism and non-Marxist socialism, its elitist revolutionary vision, its wish to create a "new man" and its centralised authoritarian party. Others reply that Aflaq was active in the Syrian–Lebanese Communist Party and the French Communist Party and was influenced by Marx. Members of Arsuzi's party read Nazi literature, and Arsuzi himself believed in the racial superiority of the Arabs; he refused Italy's advances and did not support the Axis. The Ba'ath regimes have also been accused of promoting an aggressive Arab ultranationalism, and the Mauritanian government accused the National Vanguard Party of racism.
sections.legacy:
Aflaq's views were largely synonymous with the party's ideology until the mid-1950s in Syria and the early 1960s in Iraq, and his Fi Sabil al-Ba'ath was its primary ideological book for over two decades. He is today considered the founder of the movement or at least its most notable contributor. Ba'athism sympathised with the non-aligned politics of Nehru, Nasser and Tito and opposed affiliation with either the Western or the Eastern bloc in the Cold War. In practice, Syria's state ideology became neo-Ba'athism and Iraq's was dominated by Saddamism, which fused ancient Babylonian and Assyrian heritage with Arab nationalism.

Saddam Hussein was toppled in 2003 and the Iraqi Ba'ath party was banned under the policy of De-Ba'athification. In Syria the fall of the Assad regime on 8 December 2024 ended Ba'athist rule, and the party there was dissolved in 2025. The fall of the two regimes also marked the end of its ideological influence. In Lebanon, where the Syrian party once held significant power and now derives influence from Hezbollah, organisations linked to the party face forced dissolution by the government, and very few Ba'athist groups remain in other countries, with limited influence.

summary: Ba'athism is an Arab nationalist and socialist ideology, drawn up in Syria in the 1940s by Michel Aflaq, Salah al-Din al-Bitar and Zaki al-Arsuzi, which called for a vanguard party to unite the Arab nation. Its two states, Syria and Iraq, became police states under the Assad family and Saddam Hussein, and both fell, in 2003 and 2024.
references: John F. Devlin, The Ba'th Party: A History from its origins to 1966 (Hoover Institution Press, 1975)
Raymond Hinnebusch, Syria: Revolution from Above (Routledge, 2002)
Paul Salem, Bitter Legacy: Ideology and Politics in the Arab World (Syracuse University Press, 1994)
Joseph Sassoon, Saddam Hussein's Ba'th Party: Inside an Authoritarian Regime (Cambridge University Press, 2012)
notes: Start 1940: Arsuzi's Arab Ba'ath (29 November 1940) and Aflaq and Bitar's Arab Ihya Movement (1940). End null although both regimes fell: the article says very few Ba'athist groups remain in other countries; the editor may prefer an end of 2024 (or 2025, the year the Syrian party was dissolved).
The article's section on Assadism says Assadism is 'less an ideology than a cult of personality'; I did not repeat this as a verdict.

The article gives no figures for deaths in either regime beyond approximately 400 in the 1966 coup, and nothing on the Anfal campaign, Halabja, the Hama events or the war with Iran beyond what is in the text; nothing was added from memory.
The article is inconsistent on the Arab Ihya name: it 'occasionally titled itself Arab Ba'ath during 1941'; I used Arab Ihya Movement, renamed the Arab Ba'ath Movement in 1943.

The article says the party was 'dissolved in Syria in 2025' in the lead, but the History section says only that the fall 'signals the likely demise' of the Syrian party's presence in Lebanon; I used the lead's statements.
The dyk's conversion claim: the Iraqi announcement and William Harris's report of a Western diplomat that the family knew of no conversion.

Left out: the article's passage on the Teperman interview; neo-Nazi and far-right support for Bashar al-Assad (Charlottesville, Black Lily); Saddam's admiration for Lenin, Castro, Ho Chi Minh and Tito; the Arsuzi tiger emblem and Sami al-Jundi's remark; Aflaq's views on German unification and the Arab Revolt.
'Arabization of ethnic minorities' and 'Alawitization' are the article's words.
